16.0.s.en: 1. Job rebukes his friends for their harshness

16.0.0.en: 1 Then Job answered and said, 2 "I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all. 3 Shall vain words have an end? or what emboldeneth thee that thou answerest? 4 I also could speak as ye do: if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you, and shake mine head at you. 5 But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should asswage your grief.

16.0.1.en: Then Job answered and said: "I have heard many such things.

16.0.3.en: The debate grew sharp in a painful way, until Job's ears wearied of listening to his friends, and he cried out: "I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all." This is what Job's soul had come to. The wise man says: "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with" (Prov 17:14).

16.0.4.en: Even if they speak words of comfort, they are painful, because they come from hearts that do not share his sufferings and do not feel his feelings. As the wise man says: [They sing songs to a heavy heart] (Prov 25:20), to no profit.

16.0.5.en: In the introduction of Father Hesychius of Jerusalem there is a wonderful discourse on Job's patience, especially in facing his friends who opposed him and mocked him, and he praised the virtue of patience, or longsuffering.

16.0.6.en: * A person can discover, through deep discernment, that patience is the foundation of the virtues.

16.0.7.en: Through patience Abraham became the father of nations (Gen 17:5; Sir 44:20; Rom 4:17), and the friend of God (Jas 2:23).

16.0.8.en: By patience Isaac, in the likeness of the only-begotten Son, became a sacrifice (Gen 22:2).

16.0.9.en: And by patience also Jacob carried a staff like a cross (Gen 32:10; Heb 11:21); and he who fled (Gen 27:43), patience made him return full of riches (Gen 32:22-23).

16.0.10.en: With such patience Job also struggled and raised the banner of victory, although his adversaries were many and powerful. And although he was entirely naked, he appeared as an armed man, awe-inspiring before those who wrestled with him. Job found himself cast on the ground, and those who wished to create obstacles (the demons) were circling around him in the air (Eph 2:2). Those who reviled him were clothed in purple, but he was clothed in sores. Yet the powers of the heavens counted him splendid...

16.0.11.en: The poor glorify him; the rich serve him, and all generations fixed their gaze on Job as a reflection of righteousness.

16.0.12.en: What need is there of many words about him? Do you want to learn the power of the patience that was in Job?

16.0.13.en: There were three friends who reviled him; they were healthy in body, full of vitality because of the abundance of their temporal blessings. And when they grew weary of speaking, each of them rested in turn. As for Job, he alone had his body covered with sores and his soul grieved. By his endurance he overcame these strong men, and by his patience he quieted the inflamed, chattering talk of those who insulted him, relying in vain on their chatter.

16.0.14.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * The Church repeats the words of the psalmist David: [The sinners plowed upon my back] (Ps 129:3). By this is meant that while the Church bears patiently with heretics or the lost of every kind, those whom she is able to correct, she carries on her back the works of those who commit iniquity. So when the blessed Job saw his friend Eliphaz bringing many complaints against him, accusing him of hypocrisy, he was crushed in the bitterness of the criticism, showing him to be a false comforter. By his longsuffering Job became a symbol of the Church, which in general bears such things...

16.0.15.en: Now by this answer the blessed Job points to the age of the Church, when she is seen, because of the pressure of her adversaries, to have been cast on the ground by their temporary power. Therefore it was said: "Miserable comforters are ye all" (Job 16:2), whether they are heretics or wicked men, as she looks to the good labors in the trial. When they intend to comfort her, they stir up wrong things in their minds.

16.0.17.en: * Drink mockery eagerly (willingly) as though it were the water of life. Drink it from every person, whoever he may be, as from one who wants to give you a purifying medicine that will save you from fornication. Then a star of deep purity will rise in your soul, and the lamp of God will no longer be put out in your heart.

16.0.18.en: St. John Climacus "Shall vain words have an end?

16.1.0.en: or what emboldeneth thee that thou answerest?" [3]

16.1.1.en: Job felt that they were going round in an empty circle, for they had nothing but a multitude of words without a clear aim, with nothing new and useful in them. Perhaps he counted their speech a calamity like the other calamities that had befallen him, if not worse than all the previous calamities. He felt that his friends were stirring up against him without cause, and wronging him with no benefit to themselves.

16.1.2.en: * "Shall vain words have an end?" Vain words are those that serve temporary vanity, and whose aim is not righteousness.

16.1.4.en: When a man loses true love, his heart suffers emptiness, so that he does not practice sincere friendship, but behaves in complete passivity, ignoring his suffering friends, or finding many pretexts to accuse them of evil, and instead of comforting them he disparages their persons and their conduct. Such were Job's friends in their silence as in their words!

16.1.5.en: The loss of love deprives a person of the sanctification of the two gifts, silence and speech. If he is silent, his silence carries not love but disregard for those around him, and if he speaks, he utters falsehood, and destroys himself and the souls of others.

16.1.6.en: The Holy Bible warns us against vain talk as against vain silence, so that when we are sanctified our silence is sanctified as well as our speech, and there is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silence, and both work for the edification of man and the comfort of his brethren, as for the glory of God.

16.1.7.en: "A tale out of season is as music in mourning" (Sir 22:6).

16.1.8.en: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Prov 10:19).

16.1.9.en: "A fool also multiplieth words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him?" (Eccl 10:14).

16.1.10.en: "He that useth many words shall be abhorred; and he that taketh authority unjustly shall be hated" (Sir 20:8).

16.1.11.en: "Accustom not thy mouth to coarse speech, for therein is no lack of sin" (Sir 23:17).

16.1.12.en: "Honour and shame is in talk: and the tongue of man is his fall" (Sir 5:15).

16.1.13.en: "A wise man shall be renowned by his words: and a prudent man pleaseth great men" (Sir 20:29).

16.1.14.en: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Prov 16:24).

16.1.15.en: "Refrain not to speak in the time of salvation, and hide not thy wisdom when it is fitting to display it" (Sir 4:28).

16.1.16.en: "Make not many words with a fool, and go not to him that hath no understanding" (Sir 22:14).

16.1.17.en: * The wise man is he who strives to please God, and is much in silence, and if he speaks, he speaks little, uttering what is necessary and pleasing to God.

16.1.18.en: * In silence you see your mind, but when you use your mind, you speak within yourself. For during silence the mind gives birth to the word, and the word of thanksgiving offered to God is the salvation of man.

16.1.19.en: * He who speaks foolishly has no mind, for he speaks without thinking about all things. Therefore examine what is profitable for you, for the sake of the salvation of your soul, in order to do it.

16.1.20.en: St. Anthony the Great * The mind cannot be freed from (natural) change in all things unless it goes out of the circle of itself and makes for itself a place in silence, which is higher than thought.

16.1.21.en: * The mind cannot be silent unless the body is silent, and the wall that separates them cannot be broken down except by silence and prayer.

16.1.22.en: St. Mark the Ascetic In a letter of Mar Philoxenus to the monks of Amid, which he wrote from his exile, urging them to strive for the right faith and not to be silent in bearing witness to the truth, it says:

16.1.23.en: [The monk who keeps silent about the faith out of hypocrisy does not know God.

16.1.24.en: The monk who grows lukewarm in zeal out of shame before authority does not know Christ.

16.1.25.en: The monk who is like everyone he is with (changing his colors and going along with each one) out of hypocrisy wears the face of a devil.

16.1.26.en: The monk who puts on Christ and is silent about the truth, his garment is the leprosy of Gehazi.

16.1.27.en: The monk whom grace visits and who is silent about the faith, his mouth will be stopped on the last day like the legion of demons.]

16.2.0.en: "I also could speak as ye do: if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you, and shake (move) mine head at you." [4]

16.2.1.en: What does the righteous Job desire for his friends? Did he bear hatred and enmity, and in the distress of his soul ask that what had befallen him should befall them, and that he should take the position of the comforter?

16.2.2.en: Does he desire to mock them in their trials, and shake his head at them in contempt, since shaking the head in the East is a sign of scorn (Isa 22:37; Jer 16:18; Mt 39:27)?

16.2.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what Job says is a prayer that comes from a loving man, who knows that they will not learn practical love except by entering into the experience of distress and trials. The motive is not to destroy them, but that through outward distress their hearts and inner depths may be set right.

16.2.4.en: But as for his heaping up words in the air (in vain) and mocking them by shaking his head, this is what Job does not accept, nor did he do it when they returned to him asking for prayer and for sacrifices to be offered on their behalf. What he says here is only to rebuke them and make them review themselves, that they may realize that they are uttering hollow words and mocking a suffering man! It is as though he were saying to them: it is fitting for you to do what you want others to do to you.

16.2.5.en: Moreover, since Job represents the suffering Church, she, in her love for the salvation of the wicked, asks that the Lord's rod be stretched out for discipline and not for vengeance, so that they may learn from sorrows outside how to enjoy love within.

16.2.6.en: * He says: [Oh, that your souls were in my soul's stead! And that I might comfort you with words, and shake my head at you, and move my lips for your relief] (Job 16:4-5). Sometimes it is necessary for wicked minds that cannot be corrected by the preaching of a man to be struck by God. This is what the preacher (Job) asks for them, out of tenderness toward them. For since this happens out of a great zeal of love, it is clear that he does not ask it for them as a punishment, but for the correction of the erring, so that it is a prayer for them, and not a curse against them.

16.2.7.en: The blessed Job shows in these words that he aims at this: his friends, who did not know how to sympathize with him in love in his grief, must learn by experience how they ought to be tender in the sorrows of others, and in this way live in a better inward state, understanding something about outward weakness...

16.2.8.en: Now we comfort the wicked in their falling under the rod when we point to outward sorrow for the building up of inward health in them. And we shake our heads when our mind, the leading part in us, inclines toward compassion. And we support them amid the blows of trials when we lessen the force of their sorrow with gentle words.

16.2.10.en: It is fitting for the Church, who loves all men, to practice rebuke at times, and to ask the Lord for discipline for the salvation of the fallen, and not for their destruction.

16.2.11.en: * God bears with all the weaknesses of men, but He will not allow the man who continually murmurs to be left without discipline.

16.2.12.en: * A friend who rebukes another in secret is a wise physician, but he who wants to heal before the eyes of many is in truth an abuser... The righteous man imitates God; he will not discipline a person to take revenge and vengeance for his evil, but to correct him or that others may fear.

16.2.13.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian "For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life" (Prov 6:23).

16.2.14.en: "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" (Prov 12:1).

16.2.15.en: "Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18).

16.2.16.en: "A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is made shrewd" (Prov 15:5).

16.2.17.en: "The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise" (Prov 15:31).

16.2.18.en: "He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding" (Prov 15:32).

16.2.19.en: "Open rebuke is better than secret love" (Prov 27:5).

16.2.20.en: "The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame" (Prov 29:15).

16.2.21.en: "He that hateth to be reproved is in the footsteps of the sinner: but he that feareth the Lord will repent in his heart" (Sir 21:7).

16.2.22.en: "A sinful man will not be reproved, but findeth excuses according to his desire" (Sir 32:21).

16.3.0.en: "But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should asswage your grief." [5]

16.3.1.en: Job spoke frankly with his friends: that even on the ordinary social level they had not observed the simplest rules of friendship. And that if the positions were exchanged, he could do with them what they had done with him, namely offer comforts with the mouth and tongue and pretend to words of wisdom without sharing sincere feelings. It is as though he were demanding that they exchange positions with him, even for a moment, so that they might feel the arrows they aim against him with empty words of comfort.

16.3.2.en: It was fitting for them to bind up his broken bones with their gentle words and a loving heart, not to break his bones with the violence of their hearts. The prophet Isaiah says: "The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to succour him that is weary with a word" (Isa 50:4). For one who has collapsed and become very sick needs a good ointment to support him, not stinging words that break him down all the more.

16.4.0.en: 6 "Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged: and though I forbear, what am I eased? 7 But now he hath made me weary: thou hast made desolate all my company. 8 And thou hast taken hold of me, and a witness is found; my leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face. 9 His wrath hath torn me and persecuted me; he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me. 10 They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me. 11 God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked. 12 I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark. 13 His archers compass me round about, he cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare; he poureth out my gall upon the ground. 14 He breaketh me with breach upon breach, he runneth upon me like a giant. 15 I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and thrust my horn into the dust. 16 My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death.

16.4.1.en: I have already pointed out that his lament over his condition carried wonderful prophecies about the suffering Lord Christ as Mediator and propitiatory Intercessor for us before the Father. At the same time he represents the suffering Church, which shares with her Christ His sufferings and crucifixion at the hands of those outside, as well as of the heretics who resist the divine truth.

16.4.2.en: "Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged:

16.4.3.en: and though I forbear, what am I eased?" [6]

16.4.4.en: Job was in perplexity: if he speaks, what use are his words with hard men who have no regard for his feelings; and if he is silent, does silence do away with the bitterness of his soul? If he pours out his complaint, he is accused of murmuring and misunderstood, and his grief increases. And if he is silent, he is accused of gloom. If he defends himself, they count him as clinging to self-righteousness, and if he keeps silent, they count him a wicked man who deserves greater chastisement!

16.4.5.en: The man who is earnest in his life and seeks the salvation of his soul profits from the words of the children of God, as he profits from their silence. If they speak, he receives the words in the Spirit of God for his edification, and if they are silent, he touches their inward contemplations and their enjoyment of the heavenly life. But he who in carelessness or in stubbornness seeks neither the truth nor eternal life stumbles at the words of the righteous, and also at their silence.

16.4.6.en: Job expressed the position of the Lord Christ, who, if He spoke the divine truth, was accused of being a blasphemer (Mt 26:65), and if He kept silent on the Cross, they said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save" (Mt 27:42). His soul was sorrowful unto death, not because of the pain, but for the bitterness of the sin which He bore for us in order to kill it by His death.

16.4.7.en: If the soul of the Lord Christ was sorrowful, the Church, His bride, remains groaning all the days of her sojourn until the elect complete their struggle, and the believers enjoy the fellowship of glories at the Lord's final coming.

16.4.8.en: * [What shall I do? If I speak, my grief is not taken from me, and if I bear it (in silence), it does not leave me]... No one is ignorant that this applies to the person of the blessed Job. But as for the universal Church, when she speaks, [her grief does not cease], since she does not see the wicked corrected by her words. And if she is silent, her very position of silence grieves her all the more, for while she is silent she sees the sin of the wicked increasing and exalting itself.

16.4.10.en: * Persecution is good for you, for the love of the Cross is rich in you. Torments are dear to you, for the fire of love of Him who cast His fire into the world (Lk 12:49) is ablaze in you. Your struggle is wonderful, because your persecutors are wicked. Your battle is full of wonder, because your enemies are fierce. If the pagans were persecuting you, it would be a justification for your sufferings and a relief for your torments, but now the Jews, the enemies of the Cross, line up against you. Your sufferings are higher than any sufferings, and your crown is more triumphant than any crown...

16.4.11.en: Great is the beauty of him whose sufferings are many. So the crown becomes beautiful in proportion to the severity of the affliction. The Comforter Spirit who makes you wise knows how to speak in you, and says: "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18). The affliction of a short time brings you near to keeping the everlasting life that has no end, and when you die to the world you show by death the life with Christ.

16.4.12.en: Who does not long to reap eternal life from the afflictions of time?

16.4.13.en: The world dissolves and its beauty fades, and it leaves its riches, its authority passes away and its splendor is despised, its rank is nullified and its life comes to an end, its forms change, and it is scattered like roses, and withers like flowers, and flees like a shadow, and is rolled up and hurries like a wheel, and with it pass away all the things that run in it, whether comfort or torment, honor or insult; all its properties remain with it and like it. Its afflictions do not last long, and its comfort is not real.

16.4.14.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "But now he hath made me weary.

16.5.0.en: Thou hast made desolate all my company." [7]

16.5.1.en: When Job felt the insincerity of his friends' intention, in bitterness he declared his perplexity to them, for he knows that what has befallen him is by God's permission, and so he became weary and perplexed.

16.5.2.en: He was weary of his inability to make the right decision: whether to speak or to keep silent? And Job was weary of his friends as of his very life. What added sorrows to him was the desolation of all his company. His sons and servants died, those who worked with him were scattered, and his friends became his opponents, gloating over his misfortune.

16.6.0.en: My leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face." [8]

16.6.1.en: Some of the Fathers see that Job, who is a type of the Lord Christ, sees in all that befell him only shadows of what would befall the Lord Christ. If they gathered against Job to destroy him, the powers of darkness joined together against the Lord Christ, and the sons of darkness seized Him to crucify Him, and sadly one of His disciples betrayed Him.

16.6.2.en: Job became like one seized in bitter captivity, and he became extremely lean, since his flesh wasted away because of the sores that covered his whole body; his leanness became a subject of talk proclaimed on his face, meaning that his features bore witness to the leanness he had reached.

16.6.3.en: Some translate this phrase: [Thou hast filled me with wrinkles, and this is a witness against me, and my leanness rose up against me to bear witness to my face]. His whole face became wrinkled, not because of advancing age, but because of the severity of his diseases. The sight of his face bears witness that he did not complain for nothing and without cause.

16.6.4.en: * Job proves that he gained great profit from the attack of the combatant (Satan), since the latter did not know that Job was being crowned by the very means by which he thought he was deceiving him. Therefore Job says: [Since thou hast taken hold of me, thou hast become a witness against me] (Job 16:8). For the enemy did not seize only Job's goods and his sons and daughters, but also seized Job in his own person, since the accuser took hold of him to wrestle with him and take possession of him (أ).

16.6.5.en: This is a testimony against the righteous man, accurately borne by the enemies. And so, a short time after these battles, God presented these thoughts to Job: You think that I am speaking with you in another way... but I will show forth your righteousness, you will appear as one who bears God. In every case these evils also bear testimony in Job's favor.

16.6.6.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem What happened to Job as a symbol was fulfilled in the person of the Lord Christ. And what happened with the Lord Christ opened the door for His Church to share His sufferings and crucifixion. The traitor Judas betrayed his Lord, but as for the Church, the false Antichrist remains attacking her secretly until he appears at the end of the ages to oppose her openly to her face.

16.6.7.en: It is a perpetual war between God and the devil, or between the kingdom of darkness and the kingdom of light. In ancient times Job's friends represented the kingdom of darkness, and in the days of the Lord Christ its hideousness appeared in the traitor disciple who joined with the opponents, and after the ascension of the Lord Christ into heaven the many enemies of Christ oppose her until the day when the Antichrist appears openly in a decisive and bitter battle.

16.6.8.en: * "My leanness (my falsehood) rose up against me." Job speaks of Judas, for he was the Lord's disciple (Lk 14:26-27, 33) and His apostle, but was found a liar [vain] (Jn 12:6), and a traitor (Lk 6:16).

16.6.9.en: * "It answers (challenges) to my face." When I said to my disciples: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me" (Jn 13:21), he dared to say to my face without shame: "Master, is it I?" (Mt 26:25)

16.6.10.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Satan, our enemy and adversary, will make war to keep us in his grasp. Who will escape from him? He who understands what was said of the poor and needy: [The Lord will deliver him in the day of evil] (Ps 1:41).

16.6.11.en: St. Jerome * The enemy does not kindle war against us directly and openly, but through his tricks. What are the devil's tricks? They lie in trying sometimes to capture us by short ways, but he always uses deceit... The enemy does not set temptations out in the open before us. He does not openly proclaim the worship of idols, but through his military deceits he presents opportunities for idol worship, and by enticing with words, using his skills.

16.6.12.en: St. John Chrysostom * In ordinary battles the commanders do not arm women or children or old men, but our Commander, the Lord Christ, distributes this royal weapon (which is the possession of Christ Himself) to all equally. Then He teaches them the military tricks of the devil.

16.6.13.en: Father Theodoret * Every story (of the battles of the Old Testament) contains a kind of victory and triumph over the spiritual powers of Satan.

16.6.14.en: Origen * [The liar has risen up against me, he resists me to my face.] Even in her time of peace the holy Church is subject to the liar, for many do not believe the promise of eternal life, and falsely claim to be believers. And since they cannot oppose her preaching openly, she is exposed to the liar from her back and not before her face. And when the time of evil breaks out (the days of the Antichrist), he who now makes light of the Church will stand in full awareness opposing her to her face, using plain statements with words that he borrows from the true faith.

16.6.15.en: But we must realize that when we face such things from the hands of carnal men, those who kill us violently, they are not in the violence of the evil spirit who rules their minds, as Paul says: "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world" (Eph 6:12).

16.6.17.en: * The great Savior was beaten with rods, and by the sentence passed by the governor He went out to be crucified!

16.6.18.en: He came to His own, and His own received Him not, but cast Him out from among them with scorn!

16.6.19.en: He went out to die with the wicked without any fault, then Judas repented, the lamp that was put out among his companions, and was ashamed of the evil deed he had done.

16.6.20.en: He who betrayed Him returned the silver to those who had seized Him, scorning himself, and confessed that he had betrayed Him in wickedness... And the crucifiers also fled as though they were not near, and said: What is it to us? See thou to that.

16.6.21.en: The innocent blood cast terror on those who shed it, and they began to be terrified and tremble at it before they spilled it!

16.6.22.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "His wrath hath torn me and persecuted me.

16.6.23.en: He gnasheth upon me with his teeth.

16.7.0.en: Mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me." [9]

16.7.1.en: Who is this enemy who tears him in his wrath against him? Is it Eliphaz and those with him, who crushed him by their accusations against him unjustly? Or is it Satan, who will not rest at the rest of a man who worships God in truth, so he stirs up the wicked against him?

16.7.2.en: Some see that in his weakness he sees his enemy to be God Himself, who permitted him the harsh trials, the cause of which Job does not know. If "the wrath of a king is as messengers of death" (Prov 16:14), what then would be the wrath of the King of kings? But it is clear from the context of the discourse that this is not what is meant.

16.7.3.en: * "He gathered his wrath against me, and threatened me, and gnashed his teeth upon me; mine enemy looked upon me with terrible eyes" (Job 16:9) LXX. Who are the wicked but the members of Satan? Therefore he works through them by what he puts in their hearts and they are bound to carry out. For Satan until now harbors wrath against the holy Church, but his wrath is scattered, so he places his hidden temptations through the stewardship of his members...

16.7.4.en: The teeth of this enemy are the persecutors and the executors of torments upon the righteous, who disfigure the members of the Church when they pour trials upon her elect through their persecutions of them. And the eyes of this enemy are those who plan what is to her harm for execution, and by their counsel they shed light on the cruelty of her persecutors. Therefore her ancient enemy gnashes his teeth upon her, as long as he hunts through the cruel sons of perdition the life of the righteous in her. He looks upon her with terrible eyes, through the counsels of the wicked. So he does not cease to devise trials in order to torment her more and more. And just as the incarnate Truth (the Lord Christ), in His preaching, chose poor and simple persons from the common people, so on the other side the apostate angel, the accursed man, will choose at the end of the world to preach his falsehood cunning and crooked men who have the knowledge of this world.

16.7.6.en: * Look how the Jewish nation was an adulteress!

16.7.7.en: She despised her Father and hated Him from Sinai, and when His Son became incarnate for her salvation, she seized Him and put Him on the Cross, and stood dancing and laughing and scorning and mocking.

16.7.8.en: Come, O Moses, look at the bride whom you brought out of Egypt, what she does to her pure Bridegroom!

16.7.9.en: Come, look at the feast she set before Him. She brought myrrh, she mixed vinegar, she drew the sword. Instead of manna she gave Him vinegar. Instead of the bitter waters that He made sweet for her, she put gall in the sweet waters for Him.

16.7.10.en: The chosen vine produced bad grapes.

16.7.11.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "They have gaped upon me with their mouth.

16.7.12.en: They have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully.

16.8.0.en: They have gathered themselves together against me." [10]

16.8.1.en: As for the Lord Christ, against whom all the powers of evil joined together, it was said of Him: "They gaped upon me with their mouths" (Ps 22:13), and it was said: "They shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek" (Mic 5:1), and this was fulfilled literally (Mt 26:27).

16.8.2.en: * [They smote me upon my cheek, they filled up the full measure of my punishments] (Job 16:10)... Thus the wicked smite the cheek of the holy Church when they persecute the righteous preachers.

16.8.3.en: The lost sinners think they are doing a great work when they put an end to the lives of the preachers.

16.8.4.en: After the smiting on the cheek it was fitting to say: [They filled up the full measure of my punishments], for these punishments complete their satiety, these that discipline the mind of the Church in a particular way.

16.8.6.en: * They covered His eyes and mocked Him, and struck Him with their fists, and said to Him: Prophesy to us, who is it that smote thee!

16.8.7.en: They struck with the reed the exalted Head, and the angels were terrified!

16.8.8.en: With these corrupt and evil things they repaid Him with madness...!

16.8.9.en: They became mad to veil the face of the Sun of Righteousness, lest He shine forth and the world see their corruption.

16.8.10.en: The foolish bride veiled the Bridegroom, lest He see her wickedness and corruption.

16.8.11.en: They veiled the Physician, lest He bind up their wounds and heal them!

16.8.12.en: Look at Christ, how much did He endure from the wicked?!

16.8.13.en: How did that fool dare to spit in His face!

16.8.14.en: How did you dare, O tongue, to sprinkle spittle...?!

16.8.15.en: How did you endure, O earth, the mockery of the Son...?!

16.8.16.en: A fearful sight, full of amazement, that a man should see the wax standing and spit in the face of the flame...

16.8.17.en: And this also happened for the sake of Adam, because he deserved to be spat upon for he had erred! And in place of the servant the Master rose up to receive all things!

16.8.18.en: He offered His face to receive the spittle, for He promised in Isaiah that He would not turn away His face from enduring the shame of spitting...!

16.8.19.en: The Master had pity on his weakness (Adam's), and entered Himself to receive the shame in his stead!

16.9.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked." [11]

16.9.1.en: The wicked had no authority over our Lord Jesus Christ, but since He accepted to be a sacrifice for sin for the world, out of love for mankind and obedience to the Father, the Lover of mankind, He gave them authority from above (Jn 19:11).

16.9.2.en: Such were the outlooks of the righteous Job; he counted all his life to be in the hand of the Lord, even what befell him from the wicked was by God's permission, so he says: "God hath delivered me to the ungodly." In the same spirit, when Shimei cursed the prophet David, he counted it as coming from God (2 Sam 16:5-13).

16.9.3.en: God uses even the wicked, while they enjoy their full freedom, to be a sword against their wicked brethren, or to discipline His children (Isa 10:5) or to prove them.

16.9.4.en: * Job says that this is done by "God." It is clear that he means the Father, for the only-begotten Son submitted to these (sufferings) not only of His own full will but also according to the will of His Father, for the will of the Father and the Son is one, since He wishes to complete His wonderful work for us, and to suffer for our salvation. Well then! Let us compare Job's words here with the words of the Savior...

16.9.5.en: [The Lord delivered me to the ungodly], that is, to Caiaphas, who questioned Him saying: "I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God" (Mt 26:63). And he received an answer he did not deserve, but because he adjured Him he heard this answer to his question: "Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" (Mt 26:64), and Caiaphas rent his clothes as though he were before a blasphemer.

16.9.6.en: "And turned me over into the hands of the wicked," that is, in the presence of Caiaphas and the other leaders of the Jews. For how could they not be wicked, those who cried out to Pilate: [Away with this man (to death), and release unto us Barabbas, who for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder, was cast into prison] (Lk 13:18-19).

16.10.0.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem "I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark (target)." [12]

16.10.1.en: Job was at ease in his enjoyment of the Lord's temporal goods given to him before the trial, but in the midst of the trial he felt that all that happened to him was not haphazard, nor were they chance events. It was as though God had shaken him and taken hold of his neck, as a father holds his son in his rage. As though He had chosen him out of all mankind to set him up as a mark or target at which He directs all His arrows, as though God had set him apart for this target.

16.10.2.en: * "When I was at ease he shook me, and took hold of my hair and plucked it out" (LXX). It can rightly be said that the Lord Christ calls His apostles "His hair," since they are the adornment of the head, for He was with them in peace. But when they left Christ because of the sufferings, the disciples were scattered, and therefore Job said this phrase. How was this fulfilled? Christ Himself said to His disciples: "All ye shall be offended because of me this night" (Mt 26:31)... Jesus added afterward: "For it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad" (Mt 26:31; Zech 13:7).

16.10.4.en: * We look and marvel at the Victor who stood in the court. The Son of the free who was smitten on His cheek, the Sun who embraced the pillar (around which the Lord was bound to be scourged), the Fire that is scourged with whips (Mt 27:26), the Light that is despised by darkness (Jn 8:12; 1:5), the Lord of Gabriel whom Caiaphas' servant struck (Jn 18:22), the lion's whelp whom the contemptible foxes tear (Hos 5:14).

16.10.5.en: The great Sea judged by dust.

16.10.6.en: The Fearful One who rode upon the Cherubim climbed the tree of the Cross.

16.10.7.en: The Giver of glory to the lily, and of diverse colors to the roses (Mt 6:28), hung naked in shame.

16.10.8.en: The Planter of Paradise is given vinegar and gall (Gen 2:8; Mt 27:34).

16.10.9.en: The Flame is pierced with the spear (Jn 19:34).

16.10.10.en: The Crowner of the sun with rays had a crown of thorns placed on His head (Mt 27:29).

16.10.11.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "His archers (the archers of his arrows) compass me round about.

16.10.12.en: He cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare.

16.11.0.en: He poureth out my gall upon the ground." [13]

16.11.1.en: Job counted those who contributed to the coming of his calamities as like special archers of God, to whom the divine command was issued to aim their arrows at him. And the arrows came true; they reached Job's kidneys and cleaved them asunder without mercy, as though the aim of the arrows was to kill him without pity.

16.11.2.en: "He poureth out my gall upon the ground." He took this comparison from what hunters do when they hunt a wild beast and slaughter it: they throw its gall on the ground in disgust. He counted himself as already slain, a target.

16.11.3.en: "He breaketh me with breach upon breach.

16.12.0.en: He runneth (rusheth) upon me like a giant." [14]

16.12.1.en: Job was not struck by one deadly blow, so that he might die and be at rest, but he was struck by successive blows, one blow after another, and wound upon wound. So he did not rest by dying, nor did he take breath between one blow and another, but he came to expect more, with no hope of an end to his troubles, or even of a halt at the point he had reached.

16.12.2.en: Perhaps he felt as though God were storming him like a mighty one, as cruel kings, when they conquer, bring the members of the defeated royal family, and throw them on the ground, and the king sets his foot on their necks, as a kind of enslavement, humiliation, and public disgrace.

16.12.3.en: Father Gregory (the Great) sees that Job is speaking of the enemy of good, who will not cease to storm the Church to seize the weak members as captives under his authority, and he attacks the Church like a mighty giant. The enemy wages war on the Church as a body, and also on every member in her by every possible means, in order to destroy many, if possible.

16.12.4.en: * "He breaketh me with breach upon breach." The holy Church is broken, breach upon breach, through her weak members, when sin is added to sin, until iniquity reaches a dangerous degree. This applies to one whom greed drives to theft, and theft to deceit, and he defends sin with lies...

16.12.5.en: "He meets him like a giant" (LXX). The enemy can be easily resisted if a person does not agree with him, whether in turning away from the faith or continuing in it. But if the soul has become accustomed to submit to his persuasions, then in so far as it submits to them, it becomes very hard for it to struggle against him in little or much.

16.12.6.en: Our wicked enemy "like a giant" wages war against her when she is overcome by an evil habit. But the holy Church often brings the minds of believers back to repentance, even after the commission of sins, and washes them from the practice of sins by the effectiveness of a man's disciplining himself by his own choice.

16.12.8.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh presented to us in his letter (19), which he sent to the Monastery of Mar Isaac Giyula, a vivid picture of the devil's resistance to mankind. He says that he began his war with lying (Jn 8:44) and wishes to end it with error.

16.12.9.en: In the first generation in the Garden of Eden, he cast enmity between God and His image (Adam and Eve).

16.12.10.en: And in the seventh generation he taught man fornication, and defiled the children of God (the children of pure Seth) with the daughters of Cain the outcast and their embroidered beauty.

16.12.11.en: And in the tenth generation the earth was filled with the wicked. God sent the divine Law, stretching out the hand of Moses like a lamp, to enlighten the earth that had grown dark.

16.12.12.en: And in the fourteenth generation the earth was filled with the worship of idols, and God was forgotten even in the midst of His people. So God sent Elijah the prophet, the second Moses, to declare his zeal for the glory of God against error.

16.12.13.en: And in the last times God sent His Son incarnate, and He became one of us, to make us with Him and like Him, and He gave us Himself to take us to His Father, and He descended to the bottom of the depth to raise us to the power of the height, and humbled Himself to the utmost humility in order to put to shame by his humility the wicked one who wished to become god by robbery.

16.12.14.en: * The enemy wages war to bring a man out from one form (of life) to another. And when he has brought him out of that form, he begins to make him blame himself with thoughts of gloom which Satan casts into his mind, so he thinks that he behaved badly on the day he changed his work and joined another.

16.12.15.en: He troubles him at every opportunity, and in all that he does, in order to win him over, drawing him to his cunning and contrary counsels.

16.13.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and thrust my horn into the dust." [15]

16.13.1.en: His splendid clothes no longer suited his body full of sores, nor were they fitting for one in such distress, so he sewed sackcloth for himself; he sewed the sackcloth himself, for there was no one to take pity on him and sew it for him in the midst of his severe sufferings.

16.13.2.en: The "horn" indicated authority and strength; so he himself thrust his horn into the dust, a sign of his complete rejection of any honor or exaltation. Job counted the dust to be the best place, not only to sit in the midst of, but also to bury in it his honor and authority.

16.13.3.en: * What is meant by sackcloth and ashes but repentance, and by skin and flesh but the sins of the flesh?

16.14.0.en: "My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death." [16]

16.14.1.en: Job not only lost joy, but the time became fitting to shed tears for his sins, and for the Lord's chastisements of him, and the harshness of his friends toward him, so his face became red with weeping, and his eyes bore the marks of death.

16.14.2.en: It is remarkable that Job's whole face became red, and not only his eyes, with the abundance of tears, but he did not fear death, for it had become without authority over him. He saw it as a passing shadow after Christ Himself drove the chariot of death to destroy death itself by it, and to give us the power of His resurrection. This is what the Church sings, praising the One who rose from the dead: "By His death He trampled death!"

16.14.3.en: * [On my eyelids is the shadow of death] (Job 16:16). Not death, but [the shadow of death], because the Savior is asleep. Therefore Father Jacob prophesied of the death of the Savior for our sake, uttering the following words in his blessing: [From my seed, my son, thou art gone up, thou liest down as a lion and like a whelp, and who then shall rouse him up?] (cf. Gen 49:9). For He has no need of anyone to wake Him, He who raises all mankind. He rose by Himself of His own will.

16.14.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "My eyelids are darkened" (LXX): Rightly they called by the name of eyelids those who are entrusted with guarding the safety of the paths of the feet. But the ruling guardians cannot understand the secret judgments of God; the "eyelids" of the holy Church "are darkened."

16.14.6.en: * Life made light of death, saying: [O death, where is thy sting? O Hades, where is thy victory?] (1 Cor 15:54-55).

16.14.7.en: On the day of Sunday the door of heaven was opened to them, which had been shut on Friday in the faces of the angels lest they go down to Golgotha, and they hastened to descend in their white garments, to receive our King who had saved the captives and returned to His Father.

16.14.8.en: The new tomb became the house of the wedding, built in the garden for the slain Bridegroom, who brought back the bride from the war of the enemies.

16.14.9.en: The angels in their white garments gathered and came to the Beautiful Gate, and the women disciples with their spices (Lk 23:56). Simon and John ran because of the glad tidings (Jn 20:3-8). Cleopas and his brother (Simon) had their eyes opened by the bread of blessing to see the resurrection openly. The friends uncover their faces, and the haters bow their heads.

16.14.10.en: Annas is ashamed, and Caiaphas cannot speak.

16.14.11.en: Judas is hanged, and the chiefs of the synagogue strike their faces.

16.14.12.en: The door of Hades is shut, and the door of Baptism is opened.

16.14.13.en: The Cross is set up in the watercourses.

16.14.14.en: The rational flock came to be refreshed by the waters that flowed from the Cross.

16.14.15.en: He looked at him as he was clothed with light and standing at the spring, and he conceived and gave birth in the likeness of the appearance of his beautiful light.

16.14.16.en: He put on a white garment shining like light, and made him white as snow...

16.14.17.en: The whole flock is white, for the whole Cross is clothed with light.

16.14.18.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * After Christ came and died for the life of the world, death was no longer called death, but sleep and repose.

16.14.19.en: * Do you not know how the Cross corrected many errors? Did it not destroy death, and wipe away sin, and put an end to the power of Satan, and satisfy the being of our good body? Did it not set right the whole world, and yet you do not trust in it?
